interactions.label: According to GINA criteria, bronchodilator reversibility in asthma is confirmed

params.question: According to GINA criteria, bronchodilator reversibility in asthma is confirmed when FEV1 improves by:

answers.text: At least 12% OR at least 200 mL after salbutamol

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both thresholds must be met simultaneously — a 12% rise alone, without reaching the 200 mL minimum, does not confirm reversibility.

answers.text: At least 12% AND at least 200 mL after salbutamol

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: GINA requires both a ≥12% AND ≥200 mL improvement in FEV1 after a short-acting bronchodilator to confirm the reversible obstruction characteristic of asthma.

answers.text: At least 15% AND at least 400 mL after salbutamol

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The 400 mL threshold exceeds GINA's requirement. While a 400 mL rise strongly suggests reversibility, the minimum criteria are ≥12% AND ≥200 mL.
The FEV1/FVC ratio is used to diagnose obstruction (below 0.70 post-bronchodilator), not to define reversibility. Reversibility is assessed by the absolute and percentage change in FEV1 alone.

overallFeedback.feedback: The correct answer is ≥12% AND ≥200 mL. Both criteria must be met simultaneously after a short-acting bronchodilator. This dual threshold distinguishes asthma's reversible obstruction from COPD's persistent limitation.
Correct. GINA defines reversibility as ≥12% AND ≥200 mL improvement in FEV1 — both thresholds must be met to distinguish asthma's variable obstruction from COPD's fixed obstruction.

interactions.label: In patients with chronic CO2 retention, why does uncontrolled high-flow oxygen r

params.question: In patients with chronic CO2 retention, why does uncontrolled high-flow oxygen risk worsening respiratory failure?

answers.text: It causes direct toxicity to the alveolar epithelium, accelerating emphysema

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Oxygen toxicity to alveolar epithelium requires prolonged exposure at very high concentrations and is not the acute concern in CO2 retainers. The immediate risk is loss of ventilatory drive.

answers.text: It suppresses the hypoxic ventilatory drive, allowing further CO2 accumulation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Chronic CO2 retainers lose sensitivity to carbon dioxide as a ventilatory stimulus. Their breathing drive depends on the low oxygen level sensed by the carotid bodies. High-flow oxygen removes this drive, causing hypoventilation and worsening hypercapnia.

answers.text: It increases pulmonary vascular resistance, precipitating cor pulmonale

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Oxygen therapy actually reduces pulmonary vascular resistance. The acute danger of high-flow O2 in these patients is suppression of the hypoxic drive, not a haemodynamic effect.

answers.text: It triggers reflex bronchoconstriction via the vagus nerve

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Oxygen does not cause reflex bronchoconstriction. The mechanism is central: suppression of the hypoxic ventilatory drive that has become the primary stimulus for breathing in these patients.

overallFeedback.feedback: The correct answer is suppression of the hypoxic ventilatory drive. These patients have lost their CO2 sensitivity, so their breathing depends on low oxygen levels sensed by the carotid bodies. High-flow O2 abolishes this drive, causing CO2 to rise further — which is why the safe target is 88–92% SpO2.

Correct. In chronic CO2 retainers, the carotid body hypoxic drive is the last remaining ventilatory stimulus. Flooding with oxygen removes it, worsening CO2 retention — hence the target of 88–92% SpO2.

params.question: A 55-year-old smoker's post-bronchodilator spirometry shows FEV1/FVC of 0.62 and FEV1 at 45% of predicted. What is his GOLD severity stage?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: GOLD 1 requires FEV1 ≥80% of predicted. At 45%, this patient has significantly more obstruction than the mild category allows.
GOLD 2 covers FEV1 50–79% of predicted. At 45%, this patient falls below the GOLD 2 threshold and into the next severity band.

Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.70 confirms obstruction. FEV1 at 45% of predicted falls in the 30–49% range, which is GOLD 3 (severe). This staging guides treatment escalation and prognostic counselling.
GOLD 4 requires FEV1 below 30% of predicted. At 45%, this patient is above the very severe threshold. The GOLD 3 range is 30–49%.

overallFeedback.feedback: The correct stage is GOLD 3 (severe). Remember the GOLD thresholds: ≥80% = GOLD 1, 50–79% = GOLD 2, 30–49% = GOLD 3, <30% = GOLD 4. At 45% of predicted, this patient falls in GOLD 3.
Correct. FEV1/FVC below 0.70 confirms obstruction, and FEV1 at 45% (in the 30–49% range) places this patient in GOLD 3 — severe COPD.

interactions.label: Under GINA 2023 guidelines, a short-acting beta-2 agonist alone remains the reco

params.question: Under GINA 2023 guidelines, a short-acting beta-2 agonist alone remains the recommended first-line reliever for mild asthma.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. The 2023 GINA guidelines removed SABA-only as a recommended reliever at any step. From Step 1, the preferred reliever is now low-dose ICS-formoterol, so that every rescue dose simultaneously treats the underlying airway inflammation — a paradigm shift from earlier practice.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. GINA 2023 replaced SABA-only relief with low-dose ICS-formoterol as the preferred reliever from Step 1. This ensures every rescue dose delivers anti-inflammatory therapy alongside bronchodilation, addressing the underlying inflammation even in mild asthma.

interactions.label: A 55-year-old bidi smoker with COPD has relapsed after three quit attempts. Usin

params.question: A 55-year-old bidi smoker with COPD has relapsed after three quit attempts. Using the 5As framework, which response is most appropriate?

answers.text: Warn him firmly that continued smoking will be fatal within a few years

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Fear-based counselling is less effective than empathetic, non-judgmental support. Relapse is the rule in tobacco cessation — the 5As emphasise supportive re-engagement, not scare tactics.

answers.text: Defer the conversation until he voluntarily expresses readiness to try again

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Deferring misses the opportunity to Assess and Assist. The 5As require engagement at every visit — repeated gentle offers are more effective than waiting for the patient to initiate.

answers.text: Reassess his readiness, offer pharmacotherapy, and arrange follow-up within one to two weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: After relapse, reassess readiness (Assess), offer nicotine replacement or varenicline (Assist), and arrange follow-up within one to two weeks (Arrange). Empathy and persistence, not blame, drive successful cessation.

answers.text: Advise him to switch to smokeless tobacco as a safer alternative

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Smokeless tobacco carries serious risks including oral cancer. The goal is complete tobacco cessation, not substitution with another harmful product. The 5As framework aims for a quit plan, not a product switch.

overallFeedback.feedback: The correct approach is to reassess readiness, offer pharmacotherapy, and arrange follow-up within one to two weeks. The 5As framework applies at every visit. Relapse is the rule in tobacco cessation — empathy and persistence work better than blame or deferral.

Correct. The 5As — Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange — apply at every visit, including after relapse. Empathetic, non-judgmental support with pharmacotherapy and close follow-up gives the best chance of success.
